title: Preparation and Characterization of Targeted Microbubbles
protocol: Dissolve the c(RGDfK) peptide in DMSO at a concentration of 10 mg/mL.
Prepare a methanol or chloroform solution of NHS-PEG-DSPE at a concentration of 200 mg/mL.
Add the NHS-PEG-DSPE solution to 1 mg of peptide dissolved in DMSO.
Add 3 μL of DIPEA to the mixture.
Maintain a molar ratio of at least 1:1.2 between peptide and NHS-PEG-DSPE.
Ensure a DIPEA-to-peptide molar ratio of at least 2:1 to maintain basic conditions.
Use proper protection such as gloves, labcoat, goggles, and fume hood when handling chloroform, methanol, and DIPEA.
Note that any peptide or mimetic with an unprotected N-terminus or lysine outside the binding site can be used instead of c(RGDfK).
Ensure all components are soluble in a DMSO-chloroform mixture for the reaction to proceed.
Remove volatile organic material by evaporation using a stream of nitrogen gas or a rotary evaporator, followed by overnight evaporation under high vacuum pump.
Redissolve nonvolatile residue in chloroform at 1 mg/mL for controlled sampling.
Confirm reaction completion by developing TLC plates in chloroform:methanol solvent media (2:1 v/v).
Spray TLC plates with ninhydrin and heat on a 150 °C heating block to confirm presence or absence of primary amino group.
Aliquot a sample of peptide-PEG-DSPE from chloroform, evaporate chloroform to dryness in nitrogen gas stream, then incubate under high vacuum pump.
Add saline to achieve a transparent micellar solution at 1 mg/mL concentration for further processing.
Redissolve the reaction mixture in normal saline if purification is desired.
Subject resulting micellar mixture to dialysis against normal saline and several changes of deionized water using a dialysis tubing with a molecular weight cut-off of 6-8 kDa.
Confirm completion of dialysis by conducting a conductivity check of the dialysate.
Remove the dialyzed material from the dialysis bag.
Place the removed material in a vial with a known mass.
Lyophilize the material until it reaches complete dryness.
Prepare an aqueous micellar solution of peptide-PEG-DSPE by adding dry reagent to aqueous saline.
Incubate the mixture to form small spherical micelles.
Apply sonication and use a hot water bath to accelerate the transfer from bulk state to micellar form.
Assess the quality of NHS-PEG-DSPE active ester.
Place 0.99 mL of 0.1 M sodium tetraborate buffer, pH 9.2, in a quartz or ultraviolet-transparent plastic cuvette.
Zero the spectrophotometer at 260 nm wavelength.
Add 10 μL of freshly prepared 200 mg/mL solution of NHS-PEG-DSPE in methanol to the cuvette.
Rapidly and vigorously mix the cuvette content to achieve uniformity.
Place the cuvette in the photometer, close the lid, and start the measurement.
Mark the time at the beginning of spectrophotometer measurement.
Perform continuous photometric absorbance measurements at 260 nm every 10 seconds for approximately 10 minutes or until stabilization.
Plot the kinetic curve.
Check initial A260 time points.
Extrapolate the curve to the reaction start time.
Compute the ratio between A260 at the start of the reaction and at completion of hydrolysis.
Select the proper amount of NHS-PEG-DSPE for complete modification of the primary amino group of the peptide.
Co-dissolve DSPC and PEG stearate in propylene glycol to achieve a 10 mg/mL concentration each.
Use a hot water bath to solubilize the materials.
Add 0.1 mL of this hot PG solution to a vial containing 0.85 mL of hot normal saline.
Rapidly mix the solution.
Add micellar biotin-PEG-DSPE (50 μL, 1 mg/mL in saline) at a 1:20 mass ratio to DSPC.
Heat the glass vial containing saline in a hot water bath prior to lipid addition.
Bring the vial to room temperature and place a rubber stopper on the vial, inserted halfway.
Insert PTFE capillary tubing into the vial.
Use the flow of decafluorobutane gas to fill the vial, then close the stopper while removing the capillary.
Crimp the stoppered vial at room temperature and place it in an amalgamator apparatus.
Start the amalgamator set to operate at 4300 rpm for 45 seconds.
Remove the vial with the resulting microbubbles from the amalgamator when amalgamation is completed.
Co-dissolve DSPC and PEG stearate in neat PG (10 mg/mL concentration for each material) using a hot water bath to solubilize.
Add 0.1 mL of this hot solution in PG to a vial containing 0.85 mL of hot normal saline, rapidly mix.
Add micellar peptide-PEG-DSPE (50 µL, 1 mg/mL in saline) at a 1:20 mass ratio to DSPC and mix rapidly.
Bring the vial to room temperature.
Place a rubber stopper on top of the vial, inserted halfway.
Insert polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) capillary tubing in the vial.
Use the flow of decafluorobutane gas to fill the vial.
Close the stopper and remove the capillary.
Crimp the stoppered vial.
Place the crimped vial in an amalgamator for mixing.
Bring the vial containing DSPC and PEG stearate solution to room temperature.
Add 0.1 mL of this hot PG solution to a vial with 0.89 mL of hot normal saline.
Rapidly mix the solutions.
Add 10 μL of DiI dye solution (1 mg/mL in neat PG) and mix thoroughly.
Bring the mixed vial to room temperature.
Fill the vial headspace with decafluorobutane gas as previously described.
Stopper the vial after filling.
Crimp the stoppered vial.
Amalgamate the crimped vial for mixing.
Sample an aliquot of microbubbles from the vial through the septum with an insulin syringe.
Dilute the sampled microbubble solution with a droplet of degassed saline.
Add a drop of diluted microbubble solution to a glass slide and cover it with a standard coverslip.
Perform microscopy with a video microscope equipped with a fluorescence epi-illumination, 100x oil objective, and high sensitivity video camera.
Take a sealed vial of microbubbles and place it in a conical 50 mL tube after inversion.
Centrifuge the vial in a bucket rotor for 10 minutes at 200 x g.
Remove the inverted vial from the centrifuge.
Insert a needle of an insulin syringe into the septum of the inverted vial.
Aspirate approximately 50 μL of clear infranatant slowly.
Place 2 μL of the infranatant sample in a 96-well plate.
Add 2 μL of the original lipid-PG-saline medium used to generate microbubbles to the 96-well plate.
Mix the samples with 0.1 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS):ethanol 1:1 medium containing 1% Triton X-100 in each well.
Measure the red fluorescence of DiI dye at an excitation wavelength of 555 nm and an emission wavelength of 620 nm with a fluorescence microplate reader.
Ensure that the fluorescence signal is within the linear calibration range.
Remove residual shell material by aspirating all infranatant volume after centrifugation.
Replace removed infranatant with degassed normal saline through a needle inserted into the septum.
Insert an additional long needle in the septum to reach the gas phase inside the vial and maintain it.
Connect the needle to a syringe filled with fluorocarbon gas to prevent air contact with microbubble preparation.
Invert a vial of microbubbles immediately following preparation for 15-20 minutes on a stable non-vibrating surface.
Insert an insulin syringe needle in the septum while the vial is inverted and gently collect 300-500 μL of microbubbles from the lower layer.
Maintain the needle close to the septum inner surface when drawing up samples from vials.
Pull back the syringe plunger slowly while withdrawing liquid to avoid bubble formation.
Avoid overpressure when transferring microbubble dispersion from the syringe to prevent bubble collapse.
Transfer microbubble dispersion into a small volume vial and fill with perfluorinated gas before crimping for short-term storage.
Perform particle size distribution assessment using a particle counter based on electrozone sensing or light obscuration principle.
Mix the vial gently prior to sampling to ensure representative and reproducible measurements of microbubble samples.
Sample from the center of the tested volume during measurement.
Fill a 100 mL beaker with at least 60 mL of 0.9% saline solution diluent.
Place the beaker on the stage of the electrozone sending instrument.
Lift the stage so that the tube, outer electrode plate, and stirrer are completely immersed in the diluent.
Ensure the stirrer can rotate freely.
Record the diluent electrolyte volume using a scale or metering pump.
Perform a background run to establish baseline counts.
Expect less than 5000 counts in 0.5 mL of diluent as blank for background run.
Add 10-20 µL of the microbubble mixture to the beaker.
Perform a second run after adding the microbubble mixture.
Use the background size distribution data within the software.
Subtract background run function is used to account for background particles.
Obtain the concentration of the particles in the original microbubble sample as particle number/mL, including dilution factor.
Wipe the outer surface of the pipette tip clean prior to inserting it into counting medium.
Calibrate the electrozone sensing counter for the same diluent test media used in actual tests.
Prepare the biomarker receptor surface for microbubble targeting to Petri dishes.
Use polystyrene 35 mm diameter dishes as the target surface.
Utilize nonspecific adhesion of proteins from normal saline on the polystyrene dish surface.
Employ streptavidin as a model protein for testing biotinylated bubbles that contain biotin-PEG-DSPE in their shell.
Place a droplet of streptavidin solution (0.2 mL, 10 μg/mL in PBS) in the center of each Petri dish.
Cover the droplet with a 22 mm x 22 mm plastic coverslip.
Incubate overnight at 4 °C in an enclosed moist environment to prevent drying out.
Remove the coverslips after incubation.
Wash the plates extensively with water and PBS.
Block the plates by incubating with 1.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for at least 4 h.
Use clean culture dishes blocked with 1.5% BSA as controls.
Alternatively, use recombinant αVβ3 receptor solution (e.g., at 4 µg/mL in PBS).
Deposit a droplet of microbubbles (5-20 μL) from underneath onto the target surface in an inverted Petri dish.
Allow the bubbles to float to the receptor-coated surface.
Incubate the inverted dish in a moist environment for 5-10 minutes.
Invert the dish back to its normal position.
Fill the dish with PBS.
Gently rinse to remove free microbubbles.
Perform brightfield microscopy to assess targeted adhesion.
Take a dish with receptor surface coating and fill it completely with degassed PBS-BSA buffer, extending over the top of the dish.
Inject 50 μL of bubbles into the bulk of the buffer.
Rapidly mix to achieve homogeneity while avoiding air bubble formation.
Place a segment of transparent packaging tape or culture plate sealer tape backed with a flat piece of plastic over the dish quickly and pressure-seal it.
Invert the "assembly" and place it upside down for 30 minutes.
Invert the sealed dish assembly back to a down-side-down configuration.
Remove the seal from the inverted dish.
Rinse away non-adherent microbubbles with degassed buffer solution.
Observe targeted microbubbles by microscopy or ultrasound imaging.
Incubate the inverted sealed dish at a slight angle if large bubbles are present.
Use fast flow from a micropipette tip to assess bubble adhesion during microscopy.
Test microbubble targeting in vitro using dynamic adhesion/retention assays.
Set up a parallel plate flow chamber with a custom-built inverter holder for ultrasound imaging.
Insert the chamber body with preinstalled gasket into the dish and seal it in the holder.
Use gaskets with channel height 0.127 mm and channel width 2.5 mm for the assay.
Use minimal silicon grease on the gasket for the parallel plate flow chamber assembly.
Avoid allowing grease to cover the biomarker protein-coated surface in the channel area.
Select 35 mm dishes carefully for proper sealing.
Do not screw the cap and frame of the dish-flow chamber combination too tightly.
Connect the flow tubing to a syringe pump operated in withdrawal mode.
On the feeder side, connect thin polyethylene tubing (PE50) to a vial with a dilute microbubble dispersion.
Subject the microbubble dispersion to constant mixing with a stir bar via a magnetic stirrer.
Remove air bubbles from the entire system before perfusing with microbubble-containing medium or PBS.
Adjust the pump volumetric flow rate to control the wall shear rate parameter using the formula 6Q/bh2.
Prepare a microbubble dispersion by adding a calculated volume of concentrated bubbles to the microbubble reservoir to achieve a concentration of 106 microbubbles/mL in PBS buffer with 0.1% BSA.
Place the feeder reservoir on a magnetic plate stirrer.
Insert a 1 cm x 2 cm magnetic stir bar and stir at ~400 RPM to maintain homogeneity during the course of the study.
Submerge the flow chamber assembly in degassed water and hold it in place by a weight to prevent movement during experiments.
Place the imaging probe clamped directly above the channel and tilt it at a 15° angle backwards, as well as a 5° angle clockwise to minimize specular reflection from the dish surface.
Position the flow chamber channel within the imaging plane.
Use the following imaging conditions: 15L8 transducer, contrast-specific imaging mode, dynamic range 50 dB, 7 MHz, Mechanical Index (MI) = 0.18, CPS Gain = 0.
Keep the time gain compensation uniform across the entire image.
Place the transducer face so it is touching the water surface or use a rubber protective sleeve filled with ultrasound gel.
Draw the microbubble dispersion from the reservoir through the chamber and into the pump for 2 min.
Switch the flow to PBS to remove non-adherent bubbles from the channel.
Assess acoustic backscatter of the remaining adherent (targeted) bubbles.
Increase the MI to 1.9 to destroy the adherent bubbles in the ultrasound imaging field of view.
Replace microbubble dispersion for repeated runs at high dilution.
Export individual images from the screen recording video stream before PBS flushing.
Export individual images after flushing and after destruction.
Import images into ImageJ for offline analysis.
Select the region-of-interest (ROI) to exclude inlet and outlet portions of the chamber.
Subtract the background ROI signal.
Quantify echo intensity as mean pixel intensity within ROI.
Observe adhesion of microbubbles to target surface by video microscopy.
Place parallel plate flow chamber assembly in inverted holder on microscope stage for video recording.
Count number of microbubbles bound to each target cell directly.
